We have developed a comprehensive theory for the behavior of doped graphene sheets, 
utilizing a renormalization group approach to analyze the effects of electron-electron interactions. 
Our findings indicate that the specific heat of the system is significantly influenced by the renormalized quasiparticle velocity, 
exhibiting a notable increase in the vicinity of the charge neutrality point. 
Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the system's conductivity is characterized by a non-Fermi liquid behavior, 
with the presence of a non-trivial scaling exponent. 
Our results are consistent with existing experimental data and provide a framework for understanding the behavior of doped graphene sheets. 
Additionally, our approach can be applied to other two-dimensional systems, 
such as graphene-based heterostructures and transition metal dichalcogenides. 
Our findings are expected to contribute to the ongoing research in the field of graphene and related materials.

This paper presents a novel approach to automatically identifying and eliminating
unnecessary run-time options within software systems. By leveraging a combination of
static and dynamic analysis, our method enables the removal of redundant options,
resulting in enhanced system performance and reduced complexity. Our approach is
validated through a case study involving the Apache HTTP Server, where we successfully
eliminated 20% of its run-time options. Furthermore, our method is adaptable to various
software systems, as demonstrated by its application to the Apache Tomcat web server. 
Our research contributes to the field of software engineering by providing a practical
solution for streamlining software systems. The source code for our method is available
at https://github.com/SoftwareEngineeringGroup/OptionElimination.
